Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

div1.head: Interview with William F. Nutter, Sr. [Undated]

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy
sp.p: All right. What we want to do is just start off with your name, where you were born. This is about Delawareans; so we really want to make it Delaware for you. So just start out talking with me as if we were just meeting, your name, where you were born, where you were raised, schools you went to, and then we'll get into the war aspect of it after that. When you're ready.

sp.speaker: William F. Nutter, Sr.
sp.p: All right. I was born in Wilmington at 30th and Madison Street. I was born and raised there. I went to Number 23 School first, and after we got out of Number 23 School, I went to Number 24 School over near the Washington Street bridge. After I got out of Number 24 School, I went to Warner School, which had the first year of high school in it at that time, and from there, I went to the Wilmington High School, which was on Pennsylvania Avenue, Delaware Avenue.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy
sp.p: When did you graduate from high school?

sp.speaker: William F. Nutter, Sr.
sp.p: 1935. (Discussion held off the record.)

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy
sp.p: You graduated from Wilmington High School in 1934?

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy
sp.p: Give me that --

sp.speaker: William F. Nutter, Sr.
sp.p: Yes. I graduated from Wilmington High School in 1935. From there, I took a short course in Brown -- in vocational school at 6th and French in Wilmington. They told me that I had more knowledge and I was wasting my time to stay there; so I spent a short time there, and following engines all my life, I wanted to get into airplanes. I was very interested in aircraft.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy
sp.p: Let's go back just a little bit. You said that when you went -- was it Brown Vocational --

sp.speaker: William F. Nutter, Sr.
sp.p: No. It was Wilmington Trade School back in those days, 6th and French.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy
sp.p: How did you -- did you say you already had more --

sp.speaker: William F. Nutter, Sr.
sp.p: I had been working on engines all my life, from the time I was a small child. In fact, my grandmother probably -- was right next to 23 School, and when I was a little kid, four or five years old, I'd be in the garage, and the man that owned the garage, when they dropped their wrenches, I'd go underneath the car and get the wrenches for them. So I was around it all my life, and I enjoyed working on engines. So when I went there, what they were teaching, they told me that I was just wasting my time because I was way advance of what they was already teaching at the time to the people in school. So there, I looked around and wanted to get into aviation, and I got out in the Air Service hangar at Blanker Field. That was the end of '35, in that area. And I asked them about coming there as a helper or worker, and they wouldn't take anybody on. So I asked for voluntary work, free, to learn. So I went out there and I worked there for just about a solid year.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy
sp.p: Where was that air strip?

sp.speaker: William F. Nutter, Sr.
sp.p: Air Service hangar on Blanker Field. It's on -- at Route 273, goes into New Castle. So the hangar is still there. In fact, they're going to rebuild that place. So I went there, and I got pretty well up on working on the aircraft. And then they would leave me at the weekends, and I would handle the aircraft, getting them out, whoever wanted to fly them, and preflight them and getting them ready. So after a year's time, I wasn't making any money, and my mother was spending two dollars fifty cents a week for me to get on a trolley car in Wilmington, 30th and Madison, go to Fourth Street, to Market, transfer to a bus, and go out to New Castle to the fiber mill, which was right down near (?Cammer Ford's?) place and that. From there, I walked to that place every day, snow or rain or anything. But I was just eager to learn and continued doing it. After the year, I say to my mother and father -- times were very hard back in those days. It wasn't very much work, and it was getting too much for my mother to keep keeping me; so I decided I better get out of there and find another job. So it was a nice summer weather, and it suited me nice to get out anyhow. When I did, I told my mother, "I think I've learned what I wanted, and I'm not gonna go anymore." She said, "Son, that's up to you." So I stayed home. And about after two weeks, Richard Dorsey Morgan called my home. My mother answered the phone, and he wanted to know where Bill was. She said, "Bill's not coming back anymore."

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy
sp.p: Explain to us who Richard Dorsey Morgan is.

sp.speaker: William F. Nutter, Sr.
sp.p: Richard Dorsey Morgan was the owner of Air Service Corporation on the Blanker Field. Richard Dorsey Morgan was married to Francis Du Pont at the time, and the fella that was part of the company was Johnny Mack Morgan, a brother of his, and Rand Holiday. They were the ones operating the Air Service Incorporation at that time. So when Richard Dorsey Morgan called me, my mother had taken the phone and told him I wouldn't be there anymore, he said, "Well, put him on." And I got on the phone. He said, "Well, why don't you come back?" I said, "Well, I can't keep doing this for no money, and my family's not a wealthy family. You know how times are." And he said, "Well, you come on back, and I'll give you $25 a week to start. After three months, I'll give you $35." I said, "I'm going to tell you something, Mr. Morgan. I've been there a year, maybe a little longer. I wasn't worth $25 in that year, and I ain't gonna be worth $35 in that year. I'm not gonna come back." So I'm looking for a job. And there was an ad in the paper, the Hotel du Pont want a bellhop. So I got on a trolley and went into see about that. When I got there, they said, "Well, where did you work?" I said, "Oh-oh." I said, "Well, I worked at the Air Service hangar for Richard Dorsey Morgan." He said, "Well, you're gonna have to get a recommendation." I said, "Well, I guess I'm up the creek here." So it didn't work that way. I called down there. Mr. Morgan said yes, he sent an A-1 recommendation for me, and I got the job there. Needless to say, I was making big money there, even back in those times.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy
sp.p: What was big money?

sp.speaker: William F. Nutter, Sr.
sp.p: Big money those times was 125, 150 a week. You average 60, 75 in there. But a lot of the weeks, you would make 125, 150. Most of those people back then, even though it's -- that was around '38, '39, was in there. Even back then, 50 cents on the dollar was good money, but most of those people give you at least a dollar, and when you work your shift, it was a wonderful place to be. I start paying my mother, father whatever board they wanted, and I was making enough money I bought a new convertible Packard, 1937, 120. And my father kept telling me, "Boy, you better put some of it away," but, you know, I was a young boy.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy
sp.p: So how did we go from being a bellhop at the Hotel du Pont to joining the service?

sp.speaker: William F. Nutter, Sr.
sp.p: How I got into the service, they was putting these letters in the mail to people wanting them to come in the service. And I went in and talked to a recruiting sergeant because I was interested in aircraft, and I truthfully knew at that time it was getting close to -- in the '40's, the first part of 1940. It looked like we were gonna get in the war anyhow, and I knew I had experience in aircraft and would like to get into that. So the recruiting sergeant said yes, they'd put me into that. So I went in and had to spend back then $90 to get my teeth fixed, and I'm gonna go in the service, and I got that done. When I went in there and they signed me up, there was three boys there, and I was the first one to sign, but three of us was sworn in at the same time that day. And when they signed me up, I said, "Well, wait. I got to go home and straighten some of these things out," and the colonel said, "Sir, you're in the United States service now. In two hours' time, you're going to be on a train to New York." So that's where I went from there, to Mitchel Field, Long Island, New York. And they had the old P-12 fighters and B-18 bombers back in those days. That's where I went for my basic training. Back in those days, you stayed inside for 90 days. You weren't allowed off that field. You were a recruit. And you got the pay of 21 dollars. Then you pay for your haircut and your laundry and your uniform; so you end up with 17 dollars a month was your pay. And then they were having -- after you got out of -- in 90 days, you would take an examination to qualify if you wanted to go to school. So I wanted to get on my records going to aircraft engine -- aircraft and engine school. That's A and E. So I ended up the top 20, which I had to be in. There were three, four hundred, maybe more, would take the examination, but they'd only put about 20 in the class. I was fortunate enough to get in the class. And when I graduated out of that aircraft and engine school, I had a high enough rating that I was sent to Chinook Field, Grand Tower, Illinois, for electrical electronic specialist. And I served there -- in fact, the first night I got out to Chinook Field, they give us a call, and it was eight of us called down. They said we was on KP. Be there at two o'clock in the morning. At two o'clock in the morning, we went down there, and eight of us cleaned 5,000 chickens. There's 20,000 men on that field. So needless to say, for a while, I didn't care much about eating a chicken. So finally, when we graduated from there, I asked for an extended leave to go to the next place when I got out of the school. So when I got out of the school, I got a telegram from a general saying he'd give me a couple of days' leave to go home and all. So I did that. And when I got home and went back, the first sergeant, when I walked in there, he wants to know where I'd been. He said, "You're AWOL." I said, "No, I'm not." He said, "Yes, you are." So I had this telegram from the general, and when he signed it all and said I had my leave, he didn't put "general so and so" down at the bottom. I don't think -- his first name was Bob. He just signed it "Bob." So when I handed that to that first sergeant and he saw that letter, he thought this guy was my personal friend. So I made out right good, see. I didn't have any trouble there. So then there wasn't anything at Westover Field. It was just about two buildings up, and contractors and all was just getting the hangars built. I helped put all the machinery and everything in the hangars and helped wire the field out there, a tetrahedron. That's like those wind socks only it's that big thing. They're called a tetrahedron. Wired all that up and took care of the planes in the base hangar where we were doing all this work.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy
sp.p: Where were you on December 7th? Where were you on Pearl Harbor Day?

sp.speaker: William F. Nutter, Sr.
sp.p: Or Pearl Harbor Day, I was in Westover Field. That was the field I'd been on. That's the field I told you that 25 -- B-25 airplanes come in, gonna go overseas, and I put the red crosses on the ground. I was there at that time. And I was there all the way up to December the 7th of '42, when -- that's when we shipped out overseas. When I shipped out overseas, we went on the Queen Mary December the 7th. We started out, we was almost freezing to death out there. It was 18,000 men on the Queen Mary when we went over. We got into real bad storms. We start hitting 100 foot swells. They were coming over the quarter deck in the front of the Queen Mary all day long. I had a picture of Stars and Stripes with all this record in it, but it got lost in my move and everything. We come one time of one degree of putting the Queen Mary over, turn her over. The only thing that saved it was a man in the helm, at the wheel. Instead of -- when it was rolling over, instead of trying to pull it back the other way and straighten it out, there's another hundred foot swell coming, and he kept it cut into that, and it shoved it back up. And from there on, we had to stay in areas. In fact, they give you the button. You had a red button with your number and all, and each bunch of the men would have to stay in their areas. You couldn't go out of the area or they'd put you in the brig, it was that bad out there. And I tell you we had -- I was on what they call E deck. E deck is below the water line, and they had hammocks three, four high in a room. You're just jammed in there because all the people on there. We didn't eat for three days, and everybody was getting sick. And we had a cook down there that he weighed 400, 500 pound, and he was going from both ends. And, of course, as sick as all of us was, this guy was, "Ah, a couple of you guys carry me up there and throw me overboard," and everybody laughed because you couldn't carry him up if you had to. So then we got in -- got caught in a funnel. I don't know if you guys know what a funnel was or not. The U boats made an angle across the whole Atlantic Ocean. And it went to this angle into just like the bottom of a funnel. It doesn't matter where you're going across that ocean, somewhere those U boats had you inside. And we were fortunate enough that we had the Queen Mary and it could do 33 knots, which is fast moving, but we were zig-zagging every seven seconds and we were freezing to death one night, and by morning, we were nice and warm and we was in the Azores where we were run by U-boats. But they didn't get a line on us for several reasons. That Queen Mary is just too fast for them. And we finally got over. We was supposed to take five days to go across, and it took us seven. And we landed in the Firth of Clyde up in Scotland, and the Queen Mary couldn't come in. It was too big to get to the dock. It wasn't deep enough. And we shuttled in and out of there, and then we got on those limey trains that had the pull strap windows and you sit in a little closed-in area. No lavatories. No nothing. I couldn't tell you the stories what went on, but it was something there. And we rode all day and all night to get down into England. And the place we went to was called Alconbury. We were the first group over there, 92nd Bomber Group. And we got there. It was partially built hangars that the English were using and a mud hole. In fact, where they put us down there, we was wading in mud, and we was right next to hog pens; so we called it Hog Swamp Valley where we were down in a hole. And we started out there -- well, there wasn't anything -- amount to do because we didn't have our equipment yet. Hadn't been shipped in. And we didn't have any airplanes or anything around; so they started close order drills and policing the areas and things of that type. Then it start getting a little better, and then the next thing they did, every Monday morning, we'd have Class A uniform drill, pass review with the field just back of us. Gerries got on to us, and fighters strafed that field and hit a lot of the men. So after that, that was stopped. Then we continued to go along and we had -- all of our equipment was shipped was 110 volt, 60 cycle, everything, and over in England, everything was 220/50. So we had to convert everything around. I wired up a lot of these big mansions for the officers where they'd stay. Then we started getting the airplanes in. In the first couple of runs out, we had -- we run into -- the Germans come head-on into those B-17's. You might wonder why that chin turret was put in the front of the B-17 "G" model. What was happening, the navigator and the bombardier was in the nose of the airplane. They had 50 caliber on each side, and they only could swing so far, and your flight engineer, which was an enlisted man, run the top turret. Then you had the man in the ball turret in the bottom. Neither one of them could close up. In the back, you had the waist gunner and the radio operator/gunner and then your tail gunner. So what happened, the Gerries got on to that, and they made a straight run right on the nose where you couldn't hit them, and first two or three planes we got, they use the center areas. Well, when he hit that bombardier's compartment, there's cables about that big around going up through there for all your bomb racks and everything in the front, navigation and everything else, and one hell of a mess because when we got started to work on them to repair them, they used a wire which was called varnish Cambridge back in those days. That's just a brown color, varnish color like gold. No numbers. Not anything. So it took you days of more ringing to try to match where all this has got to go back together. So we kept putting in what we call U.R., unsatisfactory reports, and we asked them to either put tracers or colors on those wires or numbers. We preferred the numbers because sometimes, you get a fella in there that's a little color blind, can't see all those different dollars. So finally, we did get that, but it was a terrible thing there. Then we got working, we had to -- a compass come out called a DR compass reading, and I had to set up the men and teach them cause I got a bunch of men that didn't know anything about these things. So I had to train those men and put all this system in. Instead of trying to get them to put the whole thing through the airplane -- it would frighten them and get them scared about trying to wire all this when you see a bundle of wires. They didn't understand, separate in your mind and follow your circuit, what you're doing. So I divided it up. Started back in the tail where the direct reading compass was, and I started a man so far, and he'd go on the junction box. That's all he'd do. Another man, he would set from there to the next one up in the junction box, and the next one would be up in the navigator's compartment. One would be up in the pilots compartment. That way, I kept them all straight, and we were able to get all that stuff in, and it was a very fast rush need.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy
sp.p: Were there any other Delawareans with you at this time?

sp.speaker: William F. Nutter, Sr.
sp.p: The only Delawareans who was with me at the time, I don't know if you looked at that pictures or not, there was four Delawareans back there. I was the only Delawarean that was in that ground force there. We started getting busy, and our fields, you know, was -- the highways or people running was just as close as right -- this highway down here? And when the cars go by and all, you didn't know what was going on or who was in there and a couple of planes, we just wired up the landing gear and get it ready, and next morning, it was cut. So they brought all of us in and questioned us. And they found out it wasn't us, and they started trying to find out what it was. Well, we started running a few more missions, and we run a few more missions. We got a lot more work, and we were working around the clock, 24 hours. And I think it was May 27th. I can look in the book and tell you exact date. We got a call one of these planes was having trouble with the engine and they wanted me over there. I was their chief troubleshooter. I said, "Well, I'll tell you. I'm taking my men down to eat." It was about six o'clock or seven o'clock at night then. "We'll have our dinner, I'm going to let them have an hour or so rest, and we'll be back up and be on them planes and find out what's what." When we got down there, we ate our dinner, we walked over to the barracks, start to lay down, and you'd think 4th of July broke loose up on that field. They were loading the bombs, and they never determined what the cause -- what caused this accident. As they'd load these bombs, they went off. Now, I have a different theory of what they did. It was a master sergeant radio technician, head technician. They were having trouble with their transmitter and everything up there, and he was up there working on that while they load these bombs. And if I'd of gone back, I'd of been in the cockpit running the engines, but the good Lord was with me, and I wasn't back. So whatever ignited these bombs -- there's one theory, they had the detonators that screwed in, a certain one. If you backed them up just a hair or so, they automatically went off. That was for when they got over in Germany, if they dropped them and they didn't go off, if somebody tried to defuse them, the defusing didn't work cause off goes the bomb. They didn't know whether that happened or whether that guy transmit electrical, which can happen easy because you see it even here today on these roads where you see construction that they'll put CB's used to be in, tell me not to transmit cause possibly could set them off. We don't know if that happened. Anyhow, it was a terrible accident. We killed a lot of men, a lot of my close friends and all, and we lost there. So we had that trouble. And while I was working there another day -- every day over there when you took off, it was approximately six to eight hundred foot of fog. Most of the guys would be taking off in just black visibility. And you only run a few seconds apart. I don't know if you've ever paid attention to any movies, but they're all just like cars at the highway, right in back of one another, and every few seconds, one is gone and another is right back, you're getting that information there. And we were going down this morning there, and this one guy, I guess he thought he was running out of the runway and all and he thought he was gonna crash up, and he stopped, gonna turn around, and three or four of them piled up there. I'll show a picture in my book there. The hangar was closer than that road out there to where my place was. And it blew that building almost apart, and all of us was running. You always run to get the men out, if you could. Everybody, all over the field, everywhere, you don't care where you were, you dropped everything and tried to save those men. Well, I made a run around the edge where that building is when she really blew good, and I had one of them sheep skin coats on and hit me right in the chest and flipped me, I don't know, ten or 15 feet back, and I thought I was all shot. It was awful pain hit me, and I peeled those coats off, looking, and there wasn't anything there. The concussion hit me. So we got those guys out, and the machine guns are going off, and, of course, you don't know if the bombs are going off. We had that happen several times. Had another one there, went down like that, and the firefighters were fighting it, and somebody said, "There's live bombs in there," and the firefighters dropped the hoses and run, and it burned the whole thing up. And they didn't realize that they could have drove out there faster on the ___ than they could get out but they got out of there. We had an awful lot of those. And I continued -- I run the electrical department all the time for -- and then I instructed around the different places on different fields. And we continuously had all kind of problems from the airplanes coming over. The people here were very new in working on aircraft. So we had a lot of young men and young women and all going in there and doing their best, but when we got planes over there, we practically had to strip them down and go over them, everything, and make sure they were flyable because these men are going six, eight, ten, 12 hours at a time, and you had to get them back. So you had to go all over those things - -- SECOND INTERVIEWER: When you getting ready to go, when you got married, he's been married already and they told you....(inaudible)

sp.speaker: William F. Nutter, Sr.
sp.p: -- I've been married. Married before. When I left -- when I was at Westover Field, I was married. I got married in Westover Field. Almost went to jail for that.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy
sp.p: Tell us the story about how you got married.

sp.speaker: William F. Nutter, Sr.
sp.p: It was a local girl. I got married because in Delaware, I was championship roller skater from Beavers Beach and all, had medals from roller skating. And when I got to Westover Field, first shot I got, near there, they had a roller skating rink; so I went there. And me being a pretty good skater, this girl over there at the first aid station, she's rolling back and forth, had her eye on me, so I went over there and asked her to skate. So I got hooked up with her this way first. I had that new convertible Packard, see. So next time I got off, I asked her to go out with me, and I didn't know that place up there. It was the evening. And when we went out, we went all up in those damn mountains and hills, and I said, "Well, what way to go home?" She was lost. So when we got back home, it was awful late at night, her mother said, "You were out with a soldier." You know, so back in our time, a solder wasn't thought of -- in 1940, '41, '42, you weren't thought of too much. So her mother wasn't very happy that she went out with me, but we kept going. And she had a wonderful mother. Really did. And I kept going with her; and finally, we decided -- I went with her, I guess, three months. We decided we're gonna get married. So I went into the office and asked the first sergeant, I said, "I want a three-day pass to get married." He says, "You can't get married. You're only a buck sergeant." See, back in those days, only first three graders, as they call them, were allowed to get married. First three graders had special seats in the theaters and all on the base. They had the privileges. I said, "Sarge, I'm gonna tell you one thing. I'm gonna get married anyhow." When I did that, he said, "Well, when you come back, you're liable to end up in the brig." I said, "I guess I will." So I went on and got married and just had the three days. Couldn't get very far away. And when I come back, I went in, and the sergeant said, "Well, did you get married?" I said, "Yeah, I got married." He said, "You know what I told you, didn't you?" I said, "Yeah. You're gonna put me in the brig, then put me in the brig." So he wrote out a payment -- I didn't know what he was writing out. He said, "Here. Go get yourself a house down in ___ circle, and here's your thing for your rations." So I made out all right there. I didn't get in any problem there - -- SECOND INTERVIEWER: Back to Delaware, when you shipped out....(Inaudible)

sp.speaker: William F. Nutter, Sr.
sp.p: -- when I shipped out, when I was leaving from up from Westover Field, my wife was pregnant. And we went down to New York where they kept us first before we're getting on the Queen Mary, and there's one of the guys that got a notice while he's there to go to officers' school; so he went back to Westover Field. He told my wife and another woman, her hus -- this man's wife, another one of the sergeants, where we were. First thing I know, we're in there and everything is secret. We're locked in. They come knocking, looking for me and this other guy. They took me up to the office. Wonder how in the devil my wife and this woman knew how to get me down here? We didn't even know they was there. This guy was going back to officers' school and told them just where to go. So we finally got that straightened out. But she was pregnant. I went on overseas.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy
sp.p: She came back to Delaware?

sp.speaker: William F. Nutter, Sr.
sp.p: When I come back, I come back to Delaware.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy
sp.p: No. Your wife. She --

sp.speaker: William F. Nutter, Sr.
sp.p: No. No. No. No. No. My wife's people lived in Springfield, Massachusetts, right close to the base, and she lived with her mother and father, and my little boy was there until I come back. And then when I come back, I was mustered out in Massachusetts and went there and then I come down here.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy
sp.p: Tell me about the fact that you didn't see your son until --

sp.speaker: William F. Nutter, Sr.
sp.p: Never got to see my son till he's two and a half years old. Yeah. And I know -- I feel sorry for the people today, but they complain a lot because they got a year. I was lucky to get back just short of three years. If I hadn't made the deal I told you, I wouldn't have got back then, probably. But it wasn't an easy time, and they didn't care. They told you you were going to stay, and that was it. See, I was a little perturbed about it because I volunteered for three years. Naturally, when the war come along, that didn't mean anything anymore. They just forgot about that. In fact, I was overseas when my mother sent me a letter -- I'd been over there about six months or a year -- that the draft board sent me a notice I was gonna be drafted. My mother asked me what she was gonna do. I said, "Well, let them draft me. I'd be happy." (Laughter.)

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy
sp.p: Wonderful. "I've been in three years already."

sp.speaker: William F. Nutter, Sr.
sp.p: I've been in all that time, they're gonna draft me. So that's what I told her.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy
sp.p: Shall we get into the book? (Discussion off the record.)

sp.speaker: William F. Nutter, Sr.
sp.p: I could tell you more about up in Westover Field, if you want.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: William F. Nutter, Sr.
sp.p: Up at Westover Field, we first got some B-24's in. When the B-24's first come in there, all of our pilots and all were not used to a tricycle gear. Everything we had was what we called tail draggers, had tail skids. So first few we got, nose wheel was busted off and coming up inside. And nobody could find the trouble; so they assigned -- I got assigned the job of trying to find this out. So I rode down in that hole in five B-24's. They had the ambulance, the fire trucks out there when we take off. And what -- we were trying to find out what was causing this. And I was down there where I could see it, but I got off to the side in case that wheel come right straight back through. You know, one of them things you had to do, and back then, I love my country and was glad to do it. It didn't bother me. A young fella, you know how young fellas are. Nothing scares them back then. So I rode down there. They go down and tell my wife, a different guy that lived in the circle, "Your husband's up there, he got the meat wagon waiting for him," and all that stuff. They do that stuff. So what I found out, I don't know if you notice these shopping carts, you ever notice the wheel when it goes like that (indicating)? This is what we was running into with these B-24's. We found out two things was causing it. When we come in, the shimmy damper had a little can on it, what's called a shimmy damper. The shock of that wheel wasn't sufficient enough. And we found out the pilots didn't know anything how to set them down. They were setting them down and letting that nose wheel at too high speed touch the ground. And when it did, it did just like that shopping cart, and it would crystallize that metal and it would sheer off and come on up through. That's what we found out there.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy
sp.p: Learn by doing kind of thing?

sp.speaker: William F. Nutter, Sr.
sp.p: Most all of it was. We didn't have many people in there that knew aircraft. We had a few, and most of those guys were old master sergeants and what we call 20 percenters. Do you know what the 20 percenter is? He's the guy when needed pay or money, he loaned it to you and when pay day come, you paid him an extra 20 percent. So we had several of those around. But wasn't many mechanics. In fact, up there, me and my buddy was going out to get two P-40's, bring them in. We had trouble with them, and we were going to repair them, and we had called the tower. We called the tower to tell them that we wouldn't have radio contact, to give us a light. You know, they have a light that they shine -- red, green, like that. So we're coming in there pretty good clip cause Westover Field is a big field. Way out there, miles of runway. And we come to this intersection of two runways. We look for a light. We got a green light. I was the first -- I was the lead airplane going in, and when I got there, I see another airplane coming on the other runway and we missed -- you couldn't put a ____ between us when the wheels turned off. So it happened to be the commanding officer in the field. So when I got the airplane stopped -- and the engine wouldn't shut off. That was the trouble with the airplane. I shut the fuel lines and all off, but it still had to feed out. And the commanding officer in the field is out there screaming and hollering for me to get out of that airplane and stand at attention. I kept telling him, "I can't shut it down," and he's hollering. So finally, it did shut off. When it shut off, I got out, and I started telling him what the trouble was. He said, "Shut up. You're under arrest." So he took me up and put me in the brig. Slammed that big iron gate, and I was in there, and I can't tell you the story what happened in there because you might not want it in that film.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy
sp.p: It's all right. We can edit it out.

sp.speaker: William F. Nutter, Sr.
sp.p: You edit this out. (Story not transcribed.)

sp.speaker: William F. Nutter, Sr.
sp.p: Anyhow, this same guy -- I've been in there three or four hours, getting late, and I had taken my brother, oldest brother, who started the one of the (?miner fire company?), one of them, not up here. He's the first charter member. And I brought him up there because the civil service people were going to take our jobs. We were going overseas. I was teaching him, and I start him off. And I tell you another story you don't put on the camera. So I'm teaching him. We had to go over to bomb site building, and then out in the shop, they had an office out there, the air brushers and all around, where the men were working and these girls were typing. So I went by this air compressor, and it didn't have a guard on it. There's a girl with a skirt on. So I called the damn officer, I said, "Lieutenant, somebody gonna get hurt there. See that compressor?" I said, "You better put a guard on it." He said, "Sergeant, I'll take care of it." I went with my brother over to the bomb site building and checked out what we had to do over there because it was all secret stuff. Come back. He had guard on it (indicating). We laughed our damn head off. He had a guard on it.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy
sp.p: An armed guard.

sp.speaker: William F. Nutter, Sr.
sp.p: An armed guard. I died laughing.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy
sp.p: That's funny.

sp.speaker: William F. Nutter, Sr.
sp.p: I'll tell you another one there.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy
sp.p: How long did it take you to get out of the brig?

sp.speaker: William F. Nutter, Sr.
sp.p: Well, to get out of the brig -- my brother went home that night. I was supposed to go home. And he told my wife, he said, "Bill is going to be working overtime tonight." So later that night, the other guy was with me, here he comes walking in with a Class A uniform on. So, shit, he got me out. So what happened, he opened the gate, closed that damn gate, and this big black guy thought it was the guy that got me in there. He grabbed ahold of him, and I had to grab him, stop him from hitting him. "That's my buddy." And it was all right then, see. Well, about ten, eleven o'clock that night, we got out. And they had a big investigation. Just like a whole board of officers, and the chief judge -- you know when you go to court -- they didn't put me on a general. They put me on a special. Special, you put a lot more time in the service. And I was really shook up. You go in there, they give me what we call a 90-day wonder. I don't know if you fellas know what they are. That's them there guys like our engineer officer, he was A & P store manager, ROTC guy. This is what I had for a lawyer, my lawyer. So we get in there and he's saying, "Oh, Christ, Commanding Officer Field." He's shaken. He's a 90-day wonder. This old colonel, he's rough. He said, "Bill, we can't do much. If it had been somebody but that Commanding Officer Field." I said, "Man, I don't want to hear that shit. I don't want to go to jail." So anyhow, he went in there, and the old man, he come down, and I belong to some organizations -- I won't tell you what -- and he happened to belong to them. Anyhow, me and this guy stand there, and the old man come around and says, "Who's Sergeant Nutter?" I said, "I am, sir," and he walked right up me and he put his nose on my face. He says, "All I want you to do is tell the truth." "Yes, sir." I get in there, and they put the old man on the stand first. So he gets up there, and he says "I was about to dig the wheels in," and he says, "I get a radio message saying you can land. Be careful of the intersection. There's two guys violating -- going on the red light." And he said, "I said, 'Well, I'll get those two guys.'" So that's what happened, I tell you, where we almost hit. Anyhow, he's starting telling him the story. Lieutenant says, "What's digging the wheels in?" He said, "Christ, man, he's landing." So anyhow, the old man get off after he tells his story, and they start my lawyer's story, and I could see the way he's hemming and hawing, stutter, scared of the colonel, my tail's going to jail. So what I did, I put my hand up, and it was a major that was the presiding judge of all the officers. I said, "Can I speak?" He said, "Yeah." I said, "Sir, I'd like to cross-examine cause this guy here, he don't know what the hell he's doing. He's gonna send me to jail." And the officers went like this. So they looked at one another, and they said, "Well, sergeant, you can't cross-examine him, but I tell you what you can do. You tell him what you want him to tell us." Now, we're standing right here, and they're there like that. So I got to tell him and then he tells him. The whole case went through, and when we got done, we went outside. About a half hour out there. The damn water's pouring off me cause I can see I'm going to jail. So they call me back in. Then they read all this history -- where you went in, volunteered in, you're married, what schools you went to, and how long you've been in the service. They go through all that shit. I'm waiting. Come on and tell me what the hell's gonna happen. So he keeps it up. Finally, he comes in and says, "You're not guilty." Then my buddy got in there. The old man come out, and he walked up and he says, "Sarge, what do you want to do with him?" I said, "Do with who?" He said, "The goddamn guy in the tower." He said, "Colonel, I don't care what the hell you do with him. I want to go home."

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy
sp.p: "He's not my concern."

sp.speaker: William F. Nutter, Sr.
sp.p: I wasn't concerned about him. You know what they did? They fined me, give him a carton of cigarettes, and sent his ass to Alaska. Well, I'll tell what you happened. The guy in the tower was an apprentice. The master sergeant in charge of the tower went downstairs to get coffee, and I didn't know these guys, how close they checked everything. Well, that light comes down to about that long, it's on a swivel. It's got a handle in the bottom. You hold it like this, like this. Back here, you shoot it. Well, they had checked everything out, had people out in the runway, and I didn't know it. That guy, when he pulled that light down, he's apprentice, when he pulled down this, held this and when this turns, it turned that thing from red to green. They had found that out, and I didn't know it, but it cost my a rank because three days after that, I was supposed to be promoted to the top grade. I never got that till almost a year later over in England. But I wasn't worried about that. I didn't go to jail. So I got out of that. Then I got into --

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy
sp.p: Let's go over to -- I want to get -- were you there at the end? Were you still in England?

sp.speaker: William F. Nutter, Sr.
sp.p: Oh, yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy
sp.p: That would have been --

sp.speaker: William F. Nutter, Sr.
sp.p: When the war -- when V-J Day, on V-J Day when the war's end, I was on a field called Pottington near Northampton in England. That was my base. I had been troubleshooting all over the 8th Air Force traveling for them, but that was my home base. And when that come out and it was over, 85 points was what you could come home on, and anybody higher would go first. Well, I had a -- I had more than the 85 plus you get so many points for your bronze star and all if you're awarded those things. I had the highest points in the outfit. So I sent my wife a nice little letter saying I'll be home pretty soon. Next day, four names went up on the board, essential to the government. I say, "Ain't no damn body essential to the government that important. Anybody else could do it." But that didn't work either. So from there, we were assigned what they called the Green Project. The Green Project, we left -- this is after Victory Day. And went to Istres, France down on the Mediterranean Sea, near Marseilles, actually. We were out in a desert, it was a converted river bed, and all turned into a desert. Dust and sand by the ton. They had -- they had those tarantulas about big around as that or bigger. They had scorpions there and malaria mosquitos, and you get in line with your musket and before you could get inside the tent with the screen, screen around it, netting, your food looked like you poured a ton of salt and pepper on it, and that's the way you had to eat it. There wasn't a tree -- one little tree one time. It's in the 92nd book. But dirt and dust, and it was terrible. And when we got down there, I went through the same procedures that I did in England. That was like our Grand Tower base in United States for the pilots. And it was all shot up and torn up by the Germans, and we had to rewire and put up buildings and everything there, and this is where I told you -- when I told you that the major was supposed to be doing all that, and that's when I made my bargain. That's how I finally ended up just short of three years getting a break to come home. I left out of there, went to 20 Grand Camp. Back then, those men being shipped home, they had all the cigarette names -- Lucky Strike, Camels, and back then, there was one called 20 Grand. That was the camp I went to, and I got a little surprise there because I was a master sergeant, and we no sooner landed the first night I got there, he said, "You're on military duty tonight." I said, "Hell, I'm not supposed to be doing that." When you got there. And we laid in there almost three months before we ever got out of there, and I come home on the U.S.S. Frederick victory ship. We were stacked on there like core wood. It took 14 days to come across. And when I got back here, that was -- in September, '45. The Red Cross, when you got off that boat, they hand you a cigarette and a donut, and that was it. Wasn't anybody around. Things had dropped off that much. Didn't get to come back soon there.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy
sp.p: Where did you land? Where did you come in?

sp.speaker: William F. Nutter, Sr.
sp.p: We come right into New York. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Thomas J. Healy
sp.p: Was your wife there to meet you?

sp.speaker: William F. Nutter, Sr.
sp.p: No. No. My wife didn't know I was getting here. No. I tell you I was gonna find out some things. But it didn't work because evidently, a few ships ahead of us come here, and some of the guys, their wives didn't know they was coming, and a couple of the wives got shot. They killed them because they were running around with men. See, I had the same idea. I was gonna find out what the hell was going on. So I didn't let anybody know I was coming home. But when I landed and all, the New York -- I guess the New York Times, one of the papers, put everybody's name, who's on these ships, so the people could go there and come through there and find out. That didn't work out. (End of interview.)
